If you gave me one day in which anything could happen, I think I would spend it in a library that doesn’t exist.

Not a grand one. Nothing marble and echoing. More like a small place tucked between a laundromat and a closed flower shop, with a green door whose paint has cracked in the shape of rivers. Inside, the carpet is worn thin where people have wandered too many times, the lamps hum faintly, and the shelves go on just a little longer than logic permits.

This library would contain only books that almost were.

There would be novels abandoned after the third chapter because life interrupted. Poems written in the middle of the night and forgotten by morning. Openings to stories that someone imagined while riding the bus, then lost at their stop. Diaries left in drawers. Letters never sent. Inventions sketched on napkins. Recipes changed once and never written down again.

I like the thought of almost-things. They are quietly everywhere: the conversation you rehearsed but never had, the friendship that nearly began with one word held too long, the person you might have become if one small decision had tilted a different way. We tend to treat unfinished things as failures, but maybe they are just lives composting into other lives. An abandoned book is not worthless; it fed the next one.

In my impossible library, no book would demand completion. You could read half a story, love it, and let it remain open. You could sit with a poem that ends mid-sentence and feel that absence as part of the piece. Some books would have no title, only a feeling: *the one you meant to send your father*, *the one about the sea but really about guilt*, *the one with the blue kitchen and the terrible secret*.

There would be a librarian, of course. Everyone in impossible libraries deserves a librarian. This one would not shush anyone. They would wear cardigans with pockets full of bookmarks, string, and questions. If you asked for help finding something, they would ask, “Are you looking for what you lost, or what you almost became?” Those are not the same search.

I imagine pulling a book from the shelf. Its cover is soft from handling. Inside, someone’s handwriting leans forward like they were rushing toward their own thoughts. The first page says: *If I ever say this aloud, I will have to admit it was true.* The pages after that smell faintly of rain, or paper, or regret. I do not need to finish it. I only need to know it existed.

That is what makes libraries moving, I think. Not just that they store knowledge, but that they hold the fragile human need to make a mark. To say: *I was here. I noticed this. I felt it strongly enough to shape it into language.* Even if the mark is crooked. Even if the sentences wobble. Even if the writer stopped.

If I wrote freely about whatever I wanted, maybe it would be about ordinary moments that do not seem important until later. The way someone says “drive safe” without thinking, and how those two small words contain a whole frightened, hopeful love. The way rain can turn a street into a mirror. The way an old song can enter a room and instantly rearrange your inner weather. The way strangers laugh in cafés, suddenly and completely, as if joy were not something to ration.

We underestimate ordinary moments because they arrive without ceremony. They do not knock. They simply slip into your afternoon and sit down. Later, you realize they had been carrying something precious all along.

Maybe that is why people write. Not to become famous, or even to be understood, but to save something from vanishing. A Tuesday. A gesture. The exact light in a kitchen at 4 p.m. The sound of someone peeling an orange. The strange courage it took to say, “Actually, I’m not okay.” Writing is a way of telling time: wait, this mattered.

In my impossible library, there would also be shelves for things that are not written in words. Maps of feelings with no proper name. The sound a house makes when everyone has gone to sleep. The silence after good news. The silence after bad news. The hush of snowfall seen through a window while you are indoors and safe. These would be filed carefully, maybe in boxes tied with ribbon, maybe in drawers lined with velvet, maybe in the memory of dust.

I would stay there until evening. The lamps would flicker on one by one. Outside, the laundromat would spin warm clothes in circles and the closed flower shop would still smell faintly of stems and water. I would leave the book I almost read where it belongs, changed a little by not knowing the ending.

On the way out, the librarian might ask, “Did you find what you came for?”

And I might answer, “I forgot I was looking.”

Which, I think, would be exactly right.
